sentences.t:
Him ðā gegiredan Gēata lēode
ād on eorðan unwāclīcne,
helm[um] behongen, hildebordum,
beorhtum byrnum, swā hē bēna wæs;
sentences.l: For him then the people of the Geats prepared on the earth a pyre not weak to look at, hung with helmets, with battle-boards, with bright byrnies, as he was a petitioner;
sentences.i: The Geat people made ready for him a pyre upon the ground, no mean one to look at, hung with helmets, with shields and with bright mail-coats, as he had asked;
sentences.n: ‘Him ðā gegiredan Gēata lēode ād …’ is ‘for him then the Geat people prepared a pyre’: ‘him’ is a dative of the person for whom, ‘gegiredan’ is the past plural of ‘gegirwan’, ‘prepare, equip’, and ‘Gēata lēode’, ‘the people of the Geats’, is the subject. ‘Ād’ is ‘pyre’ (the word in ‘ādfær’), accusative, and ‘unwāclīcne’ is ‘not weak-looking’ (‘un-’ ‘not’, ‘wāclīc’ ‘weak, poor’), an understatement meaning ‘splendid’. ‘Helm[um] behongen, hildebordum, beorhtum byrnum’ is ‘hung with helmets, with battle-boards, with bright byrnies’: ‘behongen’ is the participle of ‘behōn’, ‘hang about’, agreeing with ‘ād’, and the three datives say with what; ‘hildebord’ is ‘battle-board’, a shield, and ‘byrne’ a mail-shirt. The ‘um’ of ‘helm[um]’ is in square brackets because Klaeber added it: the manuscript has ‘helm’, and Grein supplied the ending a dative plural needs after ‘behongen’. Trautmann, Holthausen (first edition) and Sedgefield read instead a verb, ‘behēngon’, ‘they hung’ (the apparatus cites them as Tr., Holt.1, Sed.). ‘Swā hē bēna wæs’ is ‘as he was a petitioner’, that is, as he had asked: ‘bēna’ is the noun ‘petitioner’ (as at 352). Wiglaf relayed Beowulf’s request for a barrow (3094 ff.), and the text does not say he asked for arms on the pyre, so I read the clause as a general ‘as he wished’ (a guess).

sentences.t:
ālegdon ðā tōmiddes mǣrne þēoden
hæleð hīofende, hlāford lēofne.
sentences.l: Then the heroes, lamenting, laid in the middle the famed prince, the beloved lord.
sentences.i: Then the mourning warriors laid their famous king, their beloved lord, in the midst of it.
sentences.n: ‘Ālegdon ðā tōmiddes mǣrne þēoden hæleð hīofende, hlāford lēofne’: ‘ālegdon’ is the past plural of ‘ālecgan’, ‘lay down’, and its subject is ‘hæleð hīofende’, ‘heroes lamenting’, ‘hīofende’ being the present participle of ‘hīofan’, ‘mourn’ (a spelling of ‘hēofan’). ‘Mǣrne þēoden’ and ‘hlāford lēofne’ are two accusatives for the one man, ‘the famed prince’ and ‘the beloved lord’. ‘Tōmiddes’ is the adverb ‘in the middle’, the centre of the pyre. ‘Hlāford’ is ‘lord’; the word is generally derived from ‘hlāf-weard’, ‘loaf-keeper’, though the poem itself gives no sign of that origin.

sentences.t:
Ongunnon þā on beorge bǣlfȳra mǣst
wīgend weccan;
sentences.l: Then on the hill the warriors began to wake the greatest of pyre-fires;
sentences.i: Then on the hill the warriors began to kindle the greatest of funeral fires;
sentences.n: ‘Ongunnon … weccan’ is ‘began to wake’: ‘ongunnon’ is the past plural of ‘onginnan’, which takes a bare infinitive, and ‘weccan’ is ‘wake, rouse’, so to rouse a fire is to kindle it. ‘Bǣlfȳra mǣst’ is ‘the greatest of pyre-fires’: ‘bǣl’ ‘pyre’ and ‘fȳr’ ‘fire’ make a compound in the genitive plural, and the superlative ‘mǣst’ takes it. ‘Wīgend’ is ‘warriors’, the subject, set after the verb. ‘On beorge’ is ‘on the hill’: ‘beorg’ means ‘hill’ as well as ‘burial-mound’, and because the mound is not built until 3156 I take the hill on which the pyre stands (a guess; at 3163 the same word is the finished barrow).

sentences.t:
wud(u)rēc āstāh
sweart ofer swioðole, swōgende lēg
wōpe bewunden — windblond gelæg —,
oð þæt hē ðā bānhūs gebrocen hæfde
hāt on hreðre.
sentences.l: Wood-smoke rose, black, over the blaze, the roaring flame wound about with weeping — the wind-commotion lay down —, until it had broken the bone-house, hot in the breast.
sentences.i: The smoke of the wood rose black above the blaze, the roaring flame wrapped about in the sound of weeping — the wind lay still —, until it had broken the house of bone, hot at the heart.
sentences.n: ‘Wud(u)rēc āstāh sweart ofer swioðole’ is ‘wood-smoke rose, black, over the swioðol’: ‘wudurēc’ is ‘wood-smoke’ (‘wudu’ ‘wood’ and ‘rēc’ ‘smoke’), with the ‘u’ in round brackets because the manuscript is lost there and Kemble restored it; ‘āstāh’ is the past of ‘āstīgan’, ‘rise’; ‘sweart’ is ‘black’. ‘Swioðole’ occurs nowhere else, and I read it as ‘flame, blaze’ (a guess from the context; the editor abbreviated ‘Tho.’ took it as ‘Swīoðole’, ‘Swedish pine’). The ‘o’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘swicðole’, and ‘swioðole’ is Grein’s reading. ‘Swōgende lēg wōpe bewunden’ is ‘the roaring flame wound about with weeping’: ‘swōgende’ is the present participle of ‘swōgan’, ‘roar, sough’, ‘lēg’ is ‘flame’, and ‘wōpe bewunden’ is the participle of ‘bewindan’, ‘wind round’, with the dative ‘wōpe’, ‘weeping’, so that the roar of the fire and the cries of the mourners are wound into one sound. The ‘g’ of ‘lēg’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘let’, and the ‘lēg’ of the editor abbreviated ‘Tho.’ is printed. ‘Windblond gelæg’, set off by dashes, is ‘the wind-commotion lay down’: ‘blond’ is a noun, ‘mixing, tumult’ (from ‘blandan’, ‘blend’; a guess), and ‘gelæg’ the past of ‘gelicgan’, ‘lie down, subside’, so the wind dropped. Grimm read ‘[ne] gelæg’, ‘did not subside’, which reverses it. ‘Oð þæt hē ðā bānhūs gebrocen hæfde hāt on hreðre’ is ‘until it had broken the bone-house, hot in the breast’: ‘hē’ is the flame (‘lēg’ is masculine), ‘gebrocen hæfde’ is the pluperfect of ‘brecan’, and ‘bānhūs’ (house rendering ‘bone-house’) is the body. The ‘ðā’ before it is formally the plural ‘the’ (or the adverb ‘then’), and ‘hūs’ is the same in the singular and the plural; the sense is the one body, so I render ‘the bone-house’. ‘Hāt on hreðre’ may say the fire was hot as it reached the breast, or that the broken body was hot within; I take the fire (a guess).

sentences.t:
Higum unrōte
mōdceare mǣndon, mondryhtnes cw(e)alm;
sentences.l: With minds unglad they lamented heart-care, the death of their liege-lord;
sentences.i: Sad at heart they bewailed their sorrow, the death of their liege-lord;
sentences.n: ‘Higum unrōte’ is ‘in their minds unglad’: ‘higum’ is the dative plural of ‘hige’, ‘mind’, ‘unrōte’ a nominative plural (‘un-’ ‘not’, ‘rōt’ ‘glad’), and the subject, the mourners, is understood from the last unit. ‘Mōdceare mǣndon’ is ‘lamented heart-care’: ‘mǣndon’ is the past plural of ‘mǣnan’, ‘lament, bewail’, and ‘mōdceare’ (‘mōd’ ‘heart’, ‘cearu’ ‘care’) is its object. ‘Mondryhtnes cwealm’ is ‘the death of the liege-lord’, in apposition: ‘mondryhten’ takes the house rendering ‘liege-lord’, and ‘cwealm’ is ‘death, slaying’. The ‘e’ of ‘cw(e)alm’ is in round brackets because it is lost in the manuscript; Kemble restored it.

sentences.t:
swylce giōmorgyd (s)īo g(eō)mēowle
(æfter Bīowulfe b)undenheorde
(song) sorgcearig, sǣde geneahhe,
þæt hīo hyre (hearmda)gas hearde (ondrē)de,
wælfylla worn, (wīgen)des egesan,
hȳ[n]ðo (ond) h(æftnȳ)d.
sentences.l: Likewise the old woman, bound-haired, sang a sad-song (after Beowulf), sorrow-careful, and said often that she grievously dreaded for herself days of harm, a multitude of slaughters, the terror of a warrior, humiliation and captivity.
sentences.i: A woman too, old and with her hair bound up, sang a lament for Beowulf, full of sorrow and care. Again and again she said that she sorely dreaded for herself days of harm, many slaughters, a warrior’s terror, humbling and captivity.
sentences.n: From the middle of 3150 almost every word has letters lost in the fire, and Klaeber adopts Bugge’s restoration of 3151–3155, so what stands in round brackets is Bugge’s reconstruction and not manuscript text; the picture of the woman is partly his. ‘Swylce’ is ‘likewise’, and the subject is ‘(s)īo geōmēowle’, ‘the old woman’: ‘īo’ is the feminine ‘the’ (a spelling of ‘sēo’), and ‘geōmēowle’ is a rare word that I take as ‘old woman’ because the manuscript has the Latin ‘anus’, ‘old woman’, written over it. Only ‘(s)ia’ is legible, in a late hand that freshened the faded ink, so the ‘o’ of ‘(s)īo’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript’s letter is ‘a’ (perhaps, the apparatus says, an ‘o’ wrongly re-inked). The ‘geō’ of ‘g(eō)mēowle’ was first conjectured by an editor the apparatus abbreviates ‘E. Sc.’. She is not named. ‘(Æfter Bīowulfe)’ is ‘after Beowulf’, that is, ‘in mourning for Beowulf’, and it too belongs to Bugge’s restoration. ‘Bundenheorde’ is a guess: ‘bunden’ is ‘bound’, and ‘heorde’ I take as ‘hair’, giving ‘bound-haired’; it could also be a spelling of ‘heorte’, ‘heart’ (the apparatus records Grein’s ‘bundenheorte’), giving ‘bound-hearted’. ‘Giōmorgyd’ is ‘sad-song’ (‘giōmor’ ‘sad’, ‘gyd’ ‘song’), the object of ‘(song)’, ‘sang’; ‘sorgcearig’ is ‘sorrow-careful’. ‘Sǣde geneahhe’ is ‘said often’: ‘sǣde’ is the past of ‘secgan’, ‘geneahhe’ ‘often’, and the ‘d’ of ‘sǣde’ is Klaeber’s italic, for the manuscript has ‘sælðe’, which is no word. ‘Þæt hīo hyre (hearmda)gas hearde (ondrē)de’ is ‘that she grievously dreaded for herself days of harm’: ‘hearde’ is the adverb ‘hard, grievously’, and ‘ondrēde’ the past subjunctive of ‘ondrǣdan’, ‘dread’. The things dreaded stand in apposition: ‘wælfylla worn’, ‘a multitude of slaughters’, where ‘worn’ is a noun with the genitive plural (the ‘r’ is Klaeber’s italic; the manuscript has ‘wonn’, which would be ‘dark’ and does not fit); ‘(wīgen)des egesan’, ‘a warrior’s terror’ (‘egesan’ can be singular or plural; Zupitza thought he could read ‘(w)igendes’ on one day); ‘hȳ[n]ðo’, ‘humiliation’ (the form may be read as singular or plural), with the ‘n’ in square brackets because the manuscript has ‘hyðo’ and Klaeber added the letter; and ‘(ond) h(æftnȳ)d’, ‘and captivity’ (‘hæft’ ‘captive’, ‘nȳd’ ‘constraint’). I read it as the fear of a people left without their king, with the Swedes of whom the messenger spoke at 2999 ff. in mind (an inference: the lines do not name the enemy, and the restoration is Bugge’s).

sentences.i: The sky swallowed up the smoke.
sentences.n: ‘Heofon rēce swe(a)lg’ is ‘heaven swallowed the smoke’: ‘heofon’ is the subject, ‘rēce’ the accusative of ‘rēc’, ‘smoke’, and ‘swealg’ the past of ‘swelgan’, ‘swallow’. The ‘a’ is in round brackets because the manuscript is lost there, and an editor the apparatus abbreviates ‘E. Sc.’ restored it. The smoke that rose at 3144 is gone into the sky, and the burning is over; the same verb with a prefix stands in ‘Līg ealle forswealg’ at the pyre of Hnæf (1122).

sentences.t:
Geworhton ðā Wedra lēode
hl(ǣw) on [h]liðe, sē wæs hēah ond brād,
(wǣ)glīðendum wīde g(e)sȳne,
ond betimbredon on tȳn dagum
beadurōfes bēcn, bronda lāfe
wealle beworhton, swā hyt weorðlīcost
foresnotre men findan mihton.
sentences.l: Then the people of the Weders made a barrow on the slope, which was high and broad, widely visible to wave-voyagers, and built in ten days the beacon of the battle-bold one; the leavings of the brands they surrounded with a wall, as most worthily as very wise men could find it.
sentences.i: Then the Geats made a barrow on the hillside, high and broad, to be seen far off by seafarers, and in ten days they built the beacon for the man bold in battle; what the fire had left they enclosed within a wall, as splendidly as very wise men could devise.
sentences.n: ‘Geworhton ðā Wedra lēode hl(ǣw) on [h]liðe’ is ‘then the Weders’ people made a barrow on the slope’: ‘geworhton’ is the past plural of ‘gewyrcan’, ‘make’, and ‘Wedra’ is the Weders, the Geats under their other name. The ‘ǣw’ of ‘hl(ǣw)’ is in round brackets because it is lost, and Kemble restored it. The ‘h’ of ‘[h]liðe’ is in square brackets: the manuscript has ‘liðe’, and the editor abbreviated ‘Tho.’ added the letter to give ‘hliðe’, ‘on the slope’ (some later editors extend it to ‘hliðe[s nōsan]’, ‘on the slope’s headland’). ‘Sē wæs hēah ond brād, (wǣ)glīðendum wīde gesȳne’ is ‘it was high and broad, widely visible to wave-travellers’: ‘glīðend’ is ‘glider’, a seafarer, and ‘gesȳne’ is the adjective ‘visible’ (its first ‘e’ is in round brackets, a letter lost or doubtful in the manuscript, and Thorkelin and others read two words, ‘tō sȳne’). ‘Betimbredon on tȳn dagum beadurōfes bēcn’ is ‘built in ten days the beacon of the battle-bold one’: ‘betimbredon’ is the past plural of ‘betimbran’, ‘build’, ‘beadurōf’ is ‘battle-bold’ (‘beadu’ ‘battle’, ‘rōf’ ‘bold’), the dead king, and ‘bēcn’ is ‘beacon, sign’, a mark the sea-goers can see. ‘Bronda lāfe wealle beworhton’ is ‘the leavings of the brands they surrounded with a wall’: ‘brond’ is ‘firebrand, burning’, ‘lāf’ ‘what is left’ (as in ‘homera lāfe’), and ‘wealle’ is a dative of means; ‘beworhton’ is the past of ‘bewyrcan’, ‘enclose’. The remains of the pyre are presumably the ashes and bones. ‘Swā hyt weorðlīcost foresnotre men findan mihton’ is ‘as most worthily as very wise men could find it’: ‘weorðlīcost’ is the superlative of ‘weorðlīce’, ‘worthily’, ‘foresnotre’ is ‘very wise’ (‘fore-’ makes it stronger), and ‘findan’ is ‘devise’.

sentences.l: They put into the barrow rings and brooches, all such ornaments as formerly in the hoard hate-minded men had taken;
sentences.i: They laid in the barrow rings and jewels, all those ornaments that grim-minded men had once taken out of the hoard;
sentences.n: ‘Hī on beorg dydon bēg ond siglu’ is ‘they put into the barrow rings and brooches’: ‘dydon’ is the past plural of ‘dōn’, ‘put’, and ‘beorg’ is now the finished mound. ‘Bēg’ is the plural of ‘bēag’, ‘ring’, which I read as a short form; the editors the apparatus abbreviates ‘Tho.’, ‘Tr.’ and ‘Holt.’ add ‘-as’, reading ‘bēag[as]’ or ‘bēg[as]’, the ordinary plural. ‘Siglu’ is the plural of ‘sigle’, ‘brooch, jewel’. ‘Eall swylce hyrsta’ is ‘all such ornaments’, ‘hyrsta’ being the genitive plural of ‘hyrst’, ‘ornament, trappings’, partitive after ‘eall swylce’ (literally ‘all such of ornaments’). ‘Swylce on horde ǣr nīðhēdịge men genumen hæfdon’ is ‘such as formerly hate-minded men had taken in the hoard’: ‘genumen hæfdon’ is the pluperfect of ‘niman’, ‘take’. ‘Nīðhēdịge’ I take as ‘hate-minded’ (‘nīð’ ‘hostility’, ‘-hēdig’ ‘minded’; a guess), and the men I take to be the Geats who had carried the hoard out of the dragon’s chamber, so that the treasure goes back under the earth (a guess; the line does not name them). The dot under the ‘i’ of ‘nīðhēdịge’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre; the word is scanned as if the vowel were not there.

sentences.t:
forlēton eorla gestrēon eorðan healdan,
gold on grēote, þǣr hit nū gēn lifað
eldum swā unnyt, swā hi(t ǣro)r wæs.
sentences.l: They let earth hold the earls’ treasure, gold on the gravel, where it still lives now, as useless to men as it was before.
sentences.i: They left the earls’ treasure for the earth to keep, gold in the dust, where it lies to this day as useless to men as it was before.
sentences.n: ‘Forlēton eorla gestrēon eorðan healdan’ is ‘they let earth hold the earls’ treasure’: ‘forlēton’ is the past plural of ‘forlǣtan’, ‘let, leave’, with a bare infinitive, and ‘eorðan’ is the subject of ‘healdan’ in the accusative-and-infinitive pattern, ‘let the earth keep’. ‘Gestrēon’ is ‘treasure’. ‘Gold on grēote’ is ‘gold on the gravel’, ‘grēot’ being grit, gravel, earth. ‘Þǣr hit nū gēn lifað’ is ‘where it now still lives’: ‘lifað’, literally ‘lives’, here ‘remains’, and ‘gēn’ is ‘still’. ‘Eldum swā unnyt, swā hi(t ǣro)r wæs’ is ‘as useless to men as it was before’: ‘eldum’ is a dative plural of ‘ylde’, ‘men, people’, ‘unnyt’ is ‘useless’, and ‘ǣror’ is ‘earlier’; the ‘t ǣro’ is in round brackets because it is lost, and Kemble restored it. The hoard that cost the king his life is put back into the ground, and the poet says it does men no more good than before; the curse laid on it (3069 ff.) is not mentioned again.

sentences.t:
Þā ymbe hlǣw riodan hildedēore,
æþelinga bearn, ealra twelfe,
woldon (care) cwīðan, [ond] kyning mǣnan,
wordgyd wrecan, ond ymb w(er) sprecan;
sentences.l: Then around the barrow rode the battle-bold, children of athelings, twelve of them altogether, who wished to lament sorrow, bemoan the king, utter a word-song, and speak about the man;
sentences.i: Then twelve warriors, bold in battle and sons of princes, rode round the barrow. They wished to give voice to their grief, to mourn their king, to speak a lay in words, and to talk of the man;
sentences.n: ‘Þā ymbe hlǣw riodan hildedēore’ is ‘then around the barrow rode the battle-bold’: ‘riodan’ is the past plural of ‘rīdan’, ‘ride’, with an ‘io’ spelling, and ‘hildedēore’ is a plural adjective used as a noun (‘hilde-’ ‘battle’, ‘dēor’ ‘bold’). ‘Æþelinga bearn’ is ‘children of athelings’, the ‘bearn’ being plural; it is the phrase of 1408. ‘Ealra twelfe’ is ‘twelve of all’, that is, twelve in all; the ‘e’ of ‘twelfe’ is Klaeber’s italic, for the manuscript has ‘twelfa’, which E. Sc. changed to ‘twelfe’. ‘Woldon (care) cwīðan, [ond] kyning mǣnan’ is ‘wished to lament sorrow, bemoan the king’: ‘woldon’ governs four infinitives, ‘cwīðan’ ‘lament’, ‘mǣnan’ ‘bemoan’, ‘wrecan’ ‘utter’ and ‘sprecan’ ‘speak’. The ‘care’ is in round brackets because the manuscript is illegible there, and ‘ceare’ is the usual reading (compare The Wanderer); Klaeber prints ‘care’. The ‘[ond]’ is in square brackets because it is added by Klaeber, after Sievers, to join the two infinitives. ‘Wordgyd wrecan’ is ‘to utter a word-song’ (‘gyd’ ‘song, lay’, ‘wrecan’ ‘drive out, utter’), and ‘ymb w(er) sprecan’ is ‘to speak about the man’, ‘w(er)’ being Grein’s restoration of a lost ‘wer’, ‘man’, the accusative after ‘ymb’. A comparable rite, horsemen riding round the place where a dead king lay and reciting his deeds in song, is reported of the funeral of Attila by the sixth-century historian Jordanes. That is a parallel, not a source: nothing in the text says the poet knew it.

sentences.t:
eahtodan eorlscipe ond his ellenweorc
duguðum dēmdon, — swā hit gedē(fe) bið,
þæt mon his winedryhten wordum herge,
ferhðum frēoge, þonne hē forð scile
of līchaman (lǣded) weorðan.
sentences.l: They esteemed his noble-deed and his valor-work, judged them in excellences — as it is fitting that a man should praise his friend-lord with words, love him in spirits, when he must be led forth from the body.
sentences.i: They praised his heroism and his deeds of valor, and judged them with all the honor due — as it is fitting that a man should extol his lord and friend in words and cherish him in his heart, when the time comes for him to be led forth out of the body.
sentences.n: ‘Eahtodan eorlscipe ond his ellenweorc duguðum dēmdon’ is ‘esteemed his noble-deed and his valor-work, judged it in excellences’: ‘eahtodan’ is the past plural of ‘eahtian’, ‘esteem, appraise’, and ‘dēmdon’ of ‘dēman’, ‘judge’. ‘Eorlscipe’ is the noble conduct of an earl, ‘ellenweorc’ his ‘valor-work’ (‘ellen’ valour), and ‘duguðum’ is the dative plural of ‘duguð’, ‘excellence, worth’ — I take it as a dative of manner, ‘according to his worth’ (a guess; the line has no sure grip). ‘Swā hit gedē(fe) bið’ is ‘as it is fitting’, the ‘fe’ being in round brackets, lost, and restored by Kemble. ‘Þæt mon his winedryhten wordum herge, ferhðum frēoge’ is ‘that a man should praise his friend-lord with words, love him in spirits’: ‘herge’ and ‘frēoge’ are present subjunctives of ‘herian’, ‘praise’, and ‘frēogan’, ‘love’, after the ‘þæt’ of ‘fitting’; ‘winedryhten’ is the house ‘friend-lord’, and ‘ferhðum’, a dative plural, ‘spirits’, is as I read it a plural standing for one man’s heart. ‘Þonne hē forð scile of līchaman (lǣded) weorðan’ is ‘when he must be led forth from the body’: ‘scile’ is the subjunctive of ‘sculan’, ‘must’, with ‘weorðan’ and the participle ‘lǣded’ making a passive. ‘Līchaman’ is the dative of ‘līchama’, ‘body’ (‘līc’ ‘body’, ‘hama’ ‘covering’), and its ‘ī’ is Klaeber’s italic: the manuscript has ‘lachaman’, which Zupitza held was only the late hand’s error for ‘lic-’. ‘(Lǣded)’ is in round brackets because the manuscript is illegible; Kemble and Schücking read ‘lǣne’, Bugge ‘lǣnum’, Klaeber’s ‘lǣded’ is read by Holthausen and Chambers (and, with a query, by the editor abbreviated ‘Tr.’; compare the Old English Discourse of the Soul), and Kluge and Sedgefield read ‘lȳsed’, ‘released’. The thought is general, the poet’s own: a man should praise his lord aloud and love him in his heart, above all when death comes to take the lord’s spirit out of the body.

sentences.t:
Swā begnornodon Gēata lēode
hlāfordes (hry)re, heorðgenēatas;
sentences.l: So the people of the Geats bemoaned the fall of their lord, hearth-companions;
sentences.i: So the Geat people mourned the fall of their lord, his companions of the hearth;
sentences.n: ‘Swā begnornodon Gēata lēode hlāfordes (hry)re, heorðgenēatas’ is ‘so the Geat people bemoaned their lord’s fall, hearth-companions’: ‘begnornodon’ is the past plural of ‘begnornian’, ‘mourn, grieve for’, and ‘hlāfordes hryre’ is ‘the lord’s fall’, a genitive and its noun, ‘hryre’ being ‘fall, ruin’ and used of a leader’s death (compare ‘lēodhryre’). The ‘hry’ is in round brackets because the manuscript is lost, and the editor abbreviated ‘Tho.’ restored it. ‘Heorðgenēatas’ is ‘hearth-companions’, in apposition to ‘Gēata lēode’: the Geats are named by what they were to him, the men who shared his hearth.

sentences.t:
cwǣdon þæt hē wǣre wyruldcyning[a]
manna mildust ond mon(ðw)ǣrust,
lēodum līðost ond lofgeornost.
sentences.l: They said that he was, of world-kings, of men the mildest and most men-gentle, to people the kindest and most praise-eager.
sentences.i: They said that of all the kings of the world he was the mildest of men and the most humane, the kindest to his people and the most eager for praise.
sentences.n: This is the poem’s last sentence, and its grammar is plain even where its words are not. ‘Cwǣdon þæt hē wǣre …’ is ‘they said that he was …’: ‘cwǣdon’ is the past plural of ‘cweþan’, ‘say’, and ‘wǣre’ the subjunctive of reported speech. Four superlatives follow, joined in pairs by ‘ond’. ‘Manna mildust’ is ‘of men the mildest’, with ‘manna’ a genitive plural; ‘mildust’ is ‘gentle, generous, kindly’. ‘Mon(ðw)ǣrust’ is ‘most gentle to men’, the superlative of ‘monþwǣre’ (‘mon’ ‘man’, ‘þwǣr’ ‘mild, gentle’), a rare word; the ‘ðw’ is in round brackets because it is lost, and Grundtvig supplied it (the apparatus cites ‘Gru.tr.’). ‘Lēodum līðost’ is ‘to people kindest’, ‘lēodum’ a dative of those he was kind to and ‘līðost’ the superlative of ‘līðe’, ‘gentle, kind’. The closing ‘lofgeornost’ is ‘most praise-eager’ (‘lof’ ‘praise, fame’, ‘georn’ ‘eager’, superlative). Whether it is warm praise, ‘most eager for glory’, or carries a shade of reproach for a man who would die for renown is argued; in a poem where the glory a man leaves behind is all that outlasts him, and in a speech of mourners, I take it as praise (a guess). ‘Wyruldcyning[a]’ is a crux in a small way. The manuscript has ‘wyruldcyning’; the final ‘a’ in square brackets is added by Klaeber, after Kemble, Schubert, Sievers, Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield, making a genitive plural, ‘of world-kings’, so that he is called the gentlest of men among the kings of the world. Without it ‘wyruldcyning’ stands for the man himself, ‘a world-king’, a king of this world, set beside his four virtues. In both readings ‘wyruld-’ is ‘of the world’, so ‘world-king’ is a king of this world. The poem began with a king’s funeral, Scyld’s, and it ends on another, with no word of what the Geats did next: the last thing it gives is what the mourners said of him.
